purpose: The countable lists. Every entry here is finite and nameable, and every one is something a drawing can be checked against without measuring a distance. Proportions and measurements are deliberately absent -- they live in the prose, because a measured quantity was repeatedly misread in this project while a countable list was not.

body_parts.source: Hampton, Figure Drawing: Design and Invention, p10. 'It is important to be aware that you are describing the eight parts of the body.'
body_parts.note: Listed one per side so that the count matches the list. Hampton writes them as pairs -- arms (2), legs (2) -- which makes six names for eight parts, and a list whose length disagrees with its own count is the one kind of error this file must not contain.

line_kinds.source: Hampton p10. 'In this drawing process, you will never use any other type of line.'

drawing_stages.source: Hampton p35: looking for the skeleton is 'the second stage ... a transitional stage in developing volume'. Bradley's book adds detail and colour on top; Ishiwatari's thirteen-step pipeline splits the same whole into four of line and seven of colour.

fold_types.source: Bradley, Drawing People: How to Portray the Clothed Figure, ch.13.

causes.pipe: fabric falls freely from a condensed area; semicylindrical or semiconical
causes.zigzag: the inside of a bend in tubular cloth buckles; the stiffer the fabric the more angular
causes.spiral: tubular cloth condensing around a tubular form; the softer the fabric the rounder

face_parameters.source: More How To Draw Manga vol.4, Mastering Bishoujo Characters, p11: twelve types given as six opposed pairs.
face_parameters.note: These say who the character is, not whether the drawing is accurate. The eye-to-mouth distance being short is what makes a face read as a child's.

face_parts_for_combination.source: Tezuka, How to Draw Manga, p40: a table of four parts by eight variants, combined.
face_parts_for_combination.note: A face is built by combining parts, not by measuring one.

value_layers.source: comic-inking, ch.V. Objects beside each other but on different planes must not share a value.
value_layers.diagnostic: squint: a flat grey blur means a black and a white are missing

contour_jobs.source: comic-inking, ch.IV. Depth rule: heavy contour on the foreground, medium on the middle ground, fine on the background.

items: cursive (heaviest at the middle of a stroke)
angular or terse (heaviest at the end)
dead-weight (bold contour with fine interior detail)
contour_styles.source: comic-inking, ch.IV. Weights of a kind must agree with each other -- thin lines all alike, heavy lines all alike.

light_source_rule.summary: heavy line weight on the dark side of an object, thin on the light side

hair_rule.light_hair: cursive and elegant lines, weight set by the primary light source
hair_rule.dark_hair: follow the white highlight patterns; the negative space defines the hair's shape

three_dimensions_device.summary: draw an imaginary sphere around the subject and use it as the pivot; the camera, the light and the point of view all sit on that sphere
three_dimensions_device.source: Imagine FX Presents Anatomy vol.2, p62 (Ron Lemen). 'The circle is really a sphere. Ellipses with the long axis passing through circles center point.'

process_rule.summary: a rough sketch is a formal step: loose lines first, expressing the movement and the outline of the story, then inking and cleaning up, with the detail given by the variation of the line
process_rule.source: Super Anime Show 3: A Quick Study Book of Manga Sketching, ch.1-2

items: do not measure slowly -- 'the downside to slowly measuring out the figure is that it stiffens the poses' (Hampton p10)
do not let a stable symmetrical pose stand -- 'the action has either not begun, or it has ended' (Hampton p26)
do not use right angles -- 'organic shapes do not contain right angles' (comic-inking ch.VI)
do not overuse cross-hatching -- 'excessive cross-hatching is not a sign of artistic skill' (comic-inking ch.VII)

expression_layers.source: MEDIBANG, 'how to draw a deformed character's facial expression' by Tsukasan, 2021.11.21
expression_layers.note: The article starts from one face with only the eyes, mouth and brows changed, and says that is not enough. Manpu are sweat drops and anger marks; posture means a laughing person holds the belly; the parts means ribbons and hair move with the emotion -- 'for anger I made the ribbon and hair sharp like horns'. So hair, ribbons and ornaments are part of the face's work.

picture_pipeline.source: MEDIBANG, 'let us finish one picture for now' by NAKAI Nobu, 2021.12.01
picture_pipeline.note: Two rules from the same article: draw at a larger size than the finished picture will be shown and shrink it afterwards, so the drawing can be rough; and recolouring the line art is described as the only way to make a picture look elegant.

items: 1bpp (black and white only, for printed line art)
8bpp (white through grey, for coloured line art and screentone)
layer_weights.source: MEDIBANG, 'let us finish one picture for now'

pose_elements.source: CLIP STUDIO digital-art, 'using guide lines to grasp dynamics and put a soul into a pose', by Eridey
pose_elements.note: These are called the elements that do not change with style. One anti-rule sits beside them: too many action lines scatter the forces and the eye cannot settle on the most important movement, so the count is one to three, never many.

fold_material_axes.source: CLIP STUDIO digital-art, 'drawing folds by fabric: T-shirt, hoodie, shirt, suit', by miyuli
fold_material_axes.note: Folds have no fixed shape of their own; the material decides where they land and how wide they are, and they are pulled toward the seams.

items: one large in front, one small behind
composition_methods.source: MEDIBANG, 'let us think about the composition of an illustration', 2021.07.14, and 'how to place several people', 2021.03.29
composition_methods.note: The rule of thirds is the one stated with a failure case: the subject goes on one of the four intersections, and a picture whose subject sits nowhere near them leaves the viewer unable to tell what to look at. Composition is worked out on the greyscale silhouette, which is the same device as the chibi silhouette test.

canvas_ratios.source: MEDIBANG, 'let us think about the composition of an illustration'
canvas_ratios.note: Each is given with the pixel size it usually appears at and what it is used for -- 16:9 for video, 4:3 for screens, 3:2 for photographs, 1:1 for avatars.

items: let the subject break the frame
enlarge the part you most want seen
composition_devices.source: MEDIBANG, 'simple composition tips that make an illustration look better', 2021.03.15
composition_devices.note: Two of the four are stated as cause and effect: the eye is drawn to the edged area, so a margin beside the figure pulls the gaze outwards; and a tilted picture reads as unstable and moving where a frontal one reads as stable and still -- which is Hampton's 'stable, symmetrical positions keep the action in stasis' said from the picture's side rather than the body's.

items: divide the head height from crown to chin in two
draw a circle for the cranium
drop a line below the circle by half its radius
draw a vertical through the middle of the circle
drop two verticals from the circle's sides to the jaw line
attach a rectangle to the lower half of the circle -- this box is eyes, nose and jaw
mark the reference line across the circle
divide the jaw line in three
draw the face line using those guides
head_construction_steps.source: MEDIBANG, 'let us draw a front face, basic', 2021.02
head_construction_steps.note: Ten steps rather than the four-quarter circle of the girl-face article. The two agree where they overlap -- the eye line sits in the lower half -- and this one adds the cranium-and-face split, which is the distinction the skull actually has: a brain case and a facial area.

items: place the buildings as a black and white silhouette, no detail
separate each form's light, dark and middle face
pull the tone curve so the darks go darker and the lights lighter
background_steps.source: MEDIBANG, 'beautiful backgrounds using texture', and 'creating cool backgrounds'
background_steps.note: The middle step carries a countable fact: a cube seen as a cube shows three faces, never more, so a form of this kind has exactly three values to find. The background is built the same way as the figure -- silhouette first, then volume, then value -- which is the same order as the three stages.

items: palm: a box as long as it is wide
wrist: a narrow box that bends at the base of the palm
hand_forms.source: CLIP STUDIO, 'drawing hands without reference', by Stan Prokopenko
hand_forms.note: The countable part is the fingers: twelve parts excluding the thumb, which is three per finger and is the number a hand actually has. The palm's two quirks are named too -- the bone on the little-finger side is shorter so it bends nearer, and the middle finger is the longest -- and the front edge of the palm is divided in four to place where each finger grows.

items: decide what the hand is doing before drawing any of it
build the construction and place every part
add nails, creases and shadow last
hand_order.source: CLIP STUDIO, 'drawing hands without reference', by Stan Prokopenko
hand_order.note: Stated as a rule with its reason: 'before the basic construction is clear, no detail should be drawn, because a page crowded with nails, palm lines and shadow makes it hard to notice a mistake or correct one.' Two working tips sit beside it -- start from the little finger and the forefinger, because the other two then fall into place, and the line should stay pale and clean rather than scratched over.

items: all fingers as one mitten-shaped group
point and line from the joints only
finger_methods.note: Given as a choice rather than a rule: different poses suit different methods, and a mitten group is the quickest way to check how far the fingers bend together.

part_roles.source: comic-inking, ch.III, through light_source_rule. The rule names five places on a face that carry extra weight; the roles are the convention's own reading of them. Four sit under a form that overhangs -- the lid over its own underside, the nose, both lips -- so they are the shadow line (陰影線). The jaw is where the head's surface turns away from the viewer, which is the silhouette (輪郭線).
part_roles.note: **The first row of the part-x-role table, and the first fact in this file that a program reads.** The same pairs live in `lineweight/roles.py` as `PART_ROLES`, and `tools/check_learn.py` refuses a difference between the two. It says which role, not how wide -- widths are the measured half and belong in `AESTHETIC-LIBRARY.md`.

items: figure height: median 6.58 heads, range 5.15 to 6.62 over five drawings, four of them inside 6.55 to 6.62

shoulder width over head width: retired as a ratio. The two rows it had do not reproduce from their pictures, and the quantity depends on the pose -- a frontal drawing reads 2.70 and a profile 1.36, a factor of two apart
eye height within the head: 52.9 to 59.4 per cent over four drawings, median 56.2, so the head's halfway line at 50 per cent falls outside the measured range
proportion.source: measured: line drawings marked by hand, with `tools/proportion_library.py` carrying the refusal rules. What the corpus could give: 61 search results, 23 left after a saturation cut for colour, 5 of those full-length front or three-quarter views with the jaw visible -- a 22 per cent yield, so five samples for the figure height is the corpus and not the sample size that was wanted. The eye row was measured on four of those five under a written definition: head height from the outer top of the head (hair or hood, never an animal ear or a hair ornament) down to the chin, and eye height at the pupil's centre.
proportion.note: **Two of three, and the third is retired rather than pending.** The five were marked by drawing the four landmarks back onto the picture and looking again; the first attempt was out by twenty-seven per cent until that check was added. Shoulder over head is not a small sample: the two rows it had cannot be reproduced from their pictures, and the quantity moves by a factor of two between a frontal drawing and a profile, so no number of samples would turn it into a proportion. The eye row was re-measured on four drawings once its definition was written down.

part_order.source: measured: tools/line_width_library.py --regions, on two labelled drawings, in units of each figure's own height. 150605691 (pencil full figure): face 0.309, eye 0.300, boot 0.197, hair 0.194, cloth 0.165. 150609781 (grey-toned figure): eye 0.345, face 0.335, hair 0.291, dress 0.230, leg 0.229, boot 0.200.
part_order.note: **An order, and only the part of it that repeats.** Face and eye are above hair and boot in both drawings. Face against eye swaps between them (0.309 over 0.300, then 0.345 over 0.335), and hair against boot swaps too, so each pair shares a tier. A tier means the order inside it was not measured, not that it is absent -- a third drawing, a smooth outline with no interior detail, scores 1.22 between its heaviest and lightest part and is a drawing this table does not apply to. The same tiers live in `lineweight/roles.py` as `PART_TIERS`, and `tools/check_learn.py` refuses a difference.

paint_mix_operations.source: Gamblin, Painting Glossary: 'A tint is any hue (color) that has been mixed with white', 'Shade - A color mixed with black', 'Tone - A color mixed with grey'.
paint_mix_operations.note: **The second fact in this file that a program reads.** The same three names live in `lineweight/pigment.py` as `MIX_OPERATIONS`, and `tools/check_learn.py` refuses a difference, on the same argument as `part_roles`. The three are not synonyms for 'lighter' and 'darker': white raises value and lowers chroma, black lowers both, and grey lowers chroma while keeping more of the value that a shade of the same ratio spends. That last difference was measured in `tests/test_pigment.py` after a first version of the test asserted a hue claim the arithmetic did not support.

pigment_opacity_pairs.test: pull the colour down a white board and across a solid black line: 'the opaque colour obliterates the black whereas the transparent colour allows it to show through'
pigment_opacity_pairs.source: Winsor & Newton, Masterclass, 'Opaque and transparent pigments in oil painting'. Six colours, given as three same-family pairs.
pigment_opacity_pairs.note: Six colours in three same-family pairs, and the point is that the pairs are not interchangeable, and this is the list that says which is which without a measurement. **Where it changes a picture:** a transparent colour is the only one that can glaze, because a glaze is a layer that lets what is under it through; an opaque colour over the same place erases it. The pairs live in `lineweight/pigment.py` as the `opacity` column of `PIGMENTS`.

paint_brushwork_kinds.source: Gamblin, Painting Glossary; Winsor & Newton, Masterclass, 'Glazing in oils'.
paint_brushwork_kinds.note: Four ways one mark differs from another in oil, and each is defined by what it does to the layer beneath rather than by what it looks like on its own: a glaze is 'a thin, transparent layer of paint' used on top of one another to build depth and modify colours; a scumble is 'a thin or broken layer of color brushed over another so that patches of the color beneath show through'; impasto is thick and textured, which puts the mark above the surface rather than in it. **The fourth is the one the glossary does not give its own entry** -- 'dry brush' appears inside the definition of scumbling, and is kept separate here because it is the only one of the four that is about how much paint the brush is carrying.

paint_layer_rule.summary: multiple thin layers are better than fewer thicker layers, and this holds for the ground, the varnish and the paint layers alike
paint_layer_rule.source: Gamblin, 'Building Permanent Paintings', the second of ten tips.
paint_layer_rule.note: Stated by the manufacturer as a permanence rule, with the reason given elsewhere on the same page: thin layers stay flexible, and a painting that is built this way is less likely to crack. **The library arrived at the same structure for a different reason** -- every paint pass here is its own `Project`, rendered separately and stacked, because a mark placed on a flattened composite can no longer be revised. Two unrelated arguments for one arrangement is the reason to record it; neither one would have been enough on its own.

fat_over_lean.rule: the under layers of a painting should be leaner than the upper layers
fat_over_lean.reason: so that the paint film stays flexible and there will be less cracking over time
fat_over_lean.corollary: extend a colour with a mixture of solvent and binder rather than solvent alone, because solvent-only thinning makes the paint too lean to adhere
fat_over_lean.source: Gamblin, Painting Glossary (Fat, Lean, Fat-Over-Lean) and 'Building Permanent Paintings'.
fat_over_lean.note: Recorded although no code here implements it. **A rule exists in this file when it is something a picture can be checked against, not when something can be built from it** -- and this one is a check: a paint layer that was thinned with solvent alone is thinner in binder than the layer under it, which is the failure the rule names.

tinting_strength.definition: how strongly a paint changes a mixture, usually observed by adding the colour to white at a fixed ratio
tinting_strength.not: pigment load, which is the amount of pigment in the formula and cannot be read off a visual tint
depends_on: the white it is mixed into
tinting_strength.trade: a strong tint can be efficient for large mixtures and harder to control in delicate passages
tinting_strength.method: a tint ladder of at least three documented ratios rather than one arbitrary mixture
tinting_strength.source: Phoenix Art Materials, 'Opacity, Undertone and Tinting Strength: Three Ways Oil Colours Behave'. The article states its own limit: its comparison of two brands is an artist's observation, not a controlled laboratory comparison, and is not to be used for product-wide ratings.
tinting_strength.note: **This is the fact that made every `mix(a, b, t)` in the painting scripts wrong.** Those four lines interpolated by how much of each tube was scooped, which assumes two pigments move a mixture equally; the article says strength is affected by the pigment's type and by the white it is mixed into, so 'a touch' is not a quantity. `lineweight/pigment.py` carries a strength rank per pigment and `mix_by_strength` weighs by it, degenerating to the old interpolation when the strengths are equal -- so the change to a picture appears only where the pigments differ. Two axes, not one: the table keeps a pigment that is opaque and weak (cadmium yellow) beside one that is transparent and strong (ultramarine), and if a future edit ranks one column by the other, those two are what will notice.
